newsitem.title: USA: TWA probers try new tool in wreckage search.
newsitem.headline: TWA probers try new tool in wreckage search.

text.p: In a race against approaching winter weather, U.S. Navy experts will use a new sonar device to search the ocean floor for tiny remains of the TWA jet that crashed off New York in July, investigators said on Thursday.

To illustrate the complexity of the task and the size of aircraft wreckage that divers were now lifting from the Atlantic Ocean floor, an investigator showed reporters plane fragments as small as a bar of chocolate and a theatre ticket.

National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) vice-chairman Robert Francis told a media briefing that underwater recovery experts would also consider using trawling or dredging devices with suctions or blades to find wreckage.

TWA Flight 800 exploded in mid-air without warning on July 17 just 11-1/2 minutes after leaving New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport on a journey to Paris, killing all 230 passengers and crew on board. The bodies or remains of 212 people have been recovered in the months since the disaster.

Francis said the Boeing 747's centre fuel tank was still of great interest to investigators and that searchers were still looking for a fuel pump the "size of an elongated Coke can" that could be crucial. He said the top of the fuel tank was "disfigured" or "bulged" and other recovered parts of the tank were "broken up" or "shattered."

U.S. Navy Rear Adm. Edward Kristensen said the new sonar equipment could penetrate 2 inches (5 cm) to 8 inches (20 cm) of sand or silt for parts buried by storms that passed through the area in August and September. He said with good weather, the remainder of the known wreckage could be lifted within a week.

"The Grapple (the main salvage ship) could ride out heavy seas up to 10 or 12 feet (3 or 3.6 metres) but the real limitation is on the diver and the movement of the ship," Kristensen told the briefing. "I've heard it said if you get three out of five good working days it's all we can really count on."
Stormy seas and high winds halted diving operations on Thursday.
Investigators maintained there were three possible causes for the crash -- a bomb, a missile or mechanical failure -- and the lead FBI investigator vowed to see out the probe until it ended.

"We're not going to back away ever, until we come to a conclusion," said James Kallstrom, head of the FBI's New York office. "We know the plane exploded and it's one of the three reasons and there's a chance that two deal with criminality, so we're not going to abandon it."
